extracted.intended_audience: educated readers, literary critics, and students of 19th-century literature interested in evaluating poetry and novels (specifically Sir Walter Scott)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical evaluation criteria for judging an author's poetry and novels, focusing on imagination, style, characterization, use of historical material, and political/moral bearings. Aimed at assessing strengths and weaknesses in both verse and prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / attachment to the past
rubrics_metrics.description: The author is criticised for 'brooding over antiquity' and being a 'laudator temporis acti' — doting on well-authenticated superstitions and shuddering at innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong writer should project beyond mere recollection of the past, avoid excessive dependence on tradition, and not limit vision to things that 'have been.' Avoid treating the present as ignorant and the past as inherently superior; strive for original perspective rather than nostalgic repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative impulse / plastic power
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A poet is essentially a mater...he must atone for what he loses in individuality...by the energies and resources of his own mind.' The author lacks 'this creative impulse, this plastic power, this capacity of reacting on his first impressions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good poetry (and great writing generally) should transform raw materials by invention: the writer must impregnate subjects with personal imaginative force rather than merely reproducing tradition or facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of character / characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry 'wanted character' and 'slid out of the mind,' whereas the novels contain innumerable vivid, living personages (Baron of Bradwardine, Flora Maclvor, Jeanie Deans, Meg Merrilies, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be distinct, memorable, and psychologically convincing; mere picturesque names or types are insufficient. Strong characterization produces lasting impressions and emotional response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid description and spirited action
rubrics_metrics.description: The poetry 'abounded in vivid descriptions, in spirited action, in smooth and flowing versification.' Such qualities are acknowledged as real merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vividness and animated scenes are important virtues; however, they are not by themselves enough to make work memorable if other dimensions (character, imagination) are lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical mastery of versification and felicity of style
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for 'smooth and flowing versification' and a 'smooth, glossy texture' of verse; yet criticism that his ballad-rhymes can be 'meretricious' and that execution is 'light, agreeable, effeminate, diffuse.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical fluency in meter and elegant surface style are valuable, but beware of mere polish that masks superficiality. Style should serve depth and truth, not substitute for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose freshness and removal of ornamental trammels
rubrics_metrics.description: In prose the author 'has completely got rid of the trammels of authorship' and 'torn off...all the ornaments of fine writing and worn-out sentimentality' so that 'all is fresh, as from the hand of nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective prose often benefits from directness and simplicity; discarding overwrought ornament can make narrative more immediate and forceful. Aim for naturalness rather than rhetorical embellishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of authentic materials / historic/verbatim sources
rubrics_metrics.description: He 'ransacked old chronicles...squeezed out musty records...consulted wayfaring pilgrims, bed-rid sibyls' and 'has taken his materials from the original, authentic sources.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawing on concrete, authentic historical material can enrich fiction and create convincing illusion — but the author should avoid mere compilation; materials should be artistically shaped, not simply dumped onto the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism / truth of feeling and circumstance
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Facts are better than fiction; there is no romance like the romance of real life' — by arriving at what men feel, do, and say in striking situations, the work becomes 'more lively, audible, and full of vent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate depiction of human behavior and circumstance, grounded in observed fact, produces vitality. Conjuring believable habits and manners lends authenticity and emotional force to narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary power of combination / synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic asserts Sir Walter 'has no voluntary power of combination' — implying a failure to synthesize details into a higher, self-originated artistic whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond assembling materials, an author must combine elements imaginatively to achieve unity and overarching insight; mere accumulation of factual or picturesque detail is insufficient without artistic synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between background and principal figures
rubrics_metrics.description: His 'backgrounds...are more attractive than the principal figures' and 'his later works are little else but backgrounds capitally made out.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Background atmosphere and setting should enhance rather than overshadow main characters and plot; ensure principal figures and actions are at least as compelling as the scene-painting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorability and lasting impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry 'slid out of the mind as soon as read' whereas the novels make history and characters 'live over again in his volumes' — producing 'everlasting variety, truth, and freedom.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for work that endures in the reader's memory — through character, insight, emotional truth — rather than ephemeral charm that quickly fades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of setting and dialect for contrast and novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing scenes 'a century or two back' and using 'Highland manners, Northern dialect and costume' gives 'a charming and wholesome relief' to refined modern readers; Scottish settings provide bracing novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic choice of time/place and authentic dialect can create contrast that revitalizes familiar readers' perceptions; use setting to provide freshness but avoid mere exoticism without substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political and moral bearing of historical representation
rubrics_metrics.description: The novels have a 'political bearing' and the author is described as 'a professed clarifier of the age' who reconciles diversities, yet is also accused of promoting Legitimacy and romanticizing old abuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers of historical fiction should be aware of how portrayals of past societies and values influence contemporary political or moral readings; be cautious about inadvertently endorsing reactionary conclusions through nostalgic depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of meretricious ornament and superficial glitter
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that a 'glittering veil of verse' or 'meretricious' ballad-rhymes disguise weak or flimsy substance; 'tinsel common-place' translates truth of feeling into tinkling sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surface sparkle must not substitute for genuine depth. Avoid rhetorical tinsel that makes materials seem attractive but empties them of significance.
